title: The periodic table: periods, groups and blocks
html:
Guiding question

How does the periodic table help us to predict patterns and trends in the properties of elements?

Do now: write down what you think the periodic table is and what it shows. Which trends do you already know?

The periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number (Z). Because elements in the same column have the same outer electron arrangement, their properties repeat at regular intervals. This repeating pattern is called periodicity ("periodic" means occurring regularly). If you know where an element sits, you can predict its electron configuration, the ions it forms, how reactive it is, and what its oxide does in water.

S3.1.1 Periods, groups and blocks

  • Groups are the vertical columns, numbered 1–18 (IUPAC numbering). Elements in a group have the same number of valence electrons, so they have similar chemical properties.
  • Periods are the horizontal rows, numbered 1–7.
  • Blocks are named after the sublevel that holds the highest-energy (valence) electrons: the s-block (groups 1–2, plus He), the p-block (groups 13–18), the d-block (groups 3–12) and the f-block (the lanthanoids and actinoids, usually drawn as two separate rows underneath).

Named groups to know: group 1 = alkali metals; group 2 = alkaline earth metals; group 17 = halogens; group 18 = noble gases; groups 3–12 = d-block / transition elements. The f-block rows are the lanthanoids (after La) and the actinoids (after Ac). Hydrogen is placed above group 1 but is a non-metal and does not belong to any group.

Metals, metalloids and non-metals: a stepped line runs from boron down to astatine. Metals lie to the left of the line (about 80% of elements), non-metals to the right. The elements next to the line (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) are metalloids: they have properties between those of metals and non-metals, e.g. silicon is a shiny semiconductor but forms an acidic oxide.

Which element is a metalloid?

  1. Sulfur
  2. Calcium
  3. Germanium
  4. Bromine

Ge lies on the stepped line between Si and As. S and Br are non-metals; Ca is a metal.

S3.1.2 Period number, group number and electron configuration

Key pointThe period number (n) equals the number of occupied main energy levels (the outer level is n). For s- and p-block elements, the group number tells you the number of valence electrons: groups 1 and 2 have 1 and 2; groups 13–18 have (group number − 10), i.e. 3 to 8.
Common mistakeDo not say "the group number equals the number of valence electrons" for groups 13–18: chlorine is in group 17 but has 7 valence electrons. (This rule only works directly with the old 1–8 numbering of the main groups.) Helium, in group 18, has only 2.
Worked exampleDeduce the electron configuration of selenium from its position (period 4, group 16).
1. Period 4 → outer level is n = 4.
2. Group 16 → 6 valence electrons: 4s² 4p⁴.
3. Period 4 elements in the p-block have also filled the 3d sublevel.
Answer: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁴ (Z = 34 ✔).
Common mistakeBe careful with the d-block. Its elements in period 4 are filling the 3d sublevel (one less than the period number). Also remember the exceptions Cr ([Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹) and Cu ([Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹) from Structure 1.3.

Phosphorus is in group 15. How many valence electrons does it have?

Groups 13–18: valence electrons = group number − 10 = 15 − 10 = 5 (3s² 3p³).
An element is in period 3 and group 2. Identify it and give its full electron configuration

Period 3 → outer shell n = 3; group 2 → 3s². The element is magnesium: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s².

Task: create a revision mind map or quiz for the key facts of the periodic table covered so far: groups, periods, blocks, named groups, metals/non-metals/metalloids, and how to read configurations from the table.

title: Periodic trends: radius, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity
html:
S3.1.3 Periodicity: trends in atomic properties

Do now: (1) write the electron configurations of period 3 (Na to Ar); (2) what is the trend in atomic radius across the period, and why? (3) what is the trend in first ionization energy across the period, and why?

Every trend in this section is explained by the same three factors. Learn them and use them in every answer:

  1. Nuclear charge (number of protons): more protons = stronger attraction for electrons.
  2. Shielding by inner electrons: inner shells repel the outer electrons and reduce the pull they feel.
  3. Distance of the outer electrons from the nucleus (number of occupied shells): further away = weaker attraction.
Key pointAcross a period: nuclear charge increases, electrons are added to the same shell, so shielding stays about the same → outer electrons are pulled in more strongly.
Down a group: a new shell is added each time, so the outer electrons are further away and more shielded → the extra nuclear charge is outweighed and the outer electrons are held less strongly.

Atomic radius

Atomic radius (half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms of the same element):

  • Decreases across a period: greater nuclear charge, same shell, similar shielding → electrons pulled closer. In period 3, every new electron goes into the 3rd shell, so shielding does not change, but each extra proton pulls the whole electron cloud in.
  • Increases down a group: more occupied shells.
  • Noble gas radii are not usually compared because they do not form bonds with each other.

Which atom has the largest atomic radius?

  1. K
  2. Ca
  3. Na
  4. Br

K and Ca are in period 4 (four shells), and radius decreases across a period, so K is larger than Ca and Br. Na has only three shells.

Ionic radius

You need different patterns for metals (which form cations) and non-metals (which form anions).

  • Positive ions are smaller than their atoms: removing the outer electrons often removes a whole shell (Na 2,8,1 → Na⁺ 2,8), and the remaining electrons feel more pull per electron.
  • Negative ions are larger than their atoms: the extra electron(s) increase electron–electron repulsion while the nuclear charge is unchanged (Cl → Cl⁻).
  • Across period 3: Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺ (isoelectronic, 2,8, with increasing nuclear charge) and P³⁻ > S²⁻ > Cl⁻ (isoelectronic, 2,8,8). The anions are much bigger than the cations because they have an extra shell.
  • Down a group, ionic radius increases (more shells).
Compare the subatomic particles in Cl and Cl⁻. Which is smaller, and why? Predict, then reveal

Both have 17 protons. Cl has 17 electrons; Cl⁻ has 18. With the same nuclear charge but one more electron, the electron–electron repulsion increases and the electron cloud spreads out, so Cl is smaller than Cl⁻.

Exam question: a student hypothesises that P³⁺ would have an ionic radius between 110 × 10⁻¹² m (the atomic radius of P) and 212 × 10⁻¹² m (the radius of P³⁻). Evaluate this hypothesis

The hypothesis is wrong: a positive ion is smaller than its atom, so P³⁺ must be smaller than 110 × 10⁻¹² m ✓. Removing electrons increases the attraction of the nucleus for each remaining outer electron / reduces repulsion between electrons ✓. (Examiners noted that many students mistook the data-booklet value for P³⁻ as P³⁺.)

First ionization energy (IE₁)

DefinitionThe first ionization energy is the minimum energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.

Why "one mole"? Removing one electron from one atom is far too small to measure, so the value is quoted per mole. Why "gaseous"? So that the atoms are separate and there are no other forces between them to overcome.

Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻    IE₁ = +496 kJ mol⁻¹
  • General increase across a period: greater nuclear charge, same shell, similar shielding → outer electron held more tightly.
  • Decrease down a group: outer electron further from the nucleus and more shielded.
  • The 2nd IE removes the second electron from a 1+ ion (Na⁺(g) → Na²⁺(g) + e⁻); it does not remove two electrons at once.

Which equation represents the first ionization energy of magnesium?

  1. Mg(s) → Mg⁺(s) + e⁻
  2. Mg(g) → Mg⁺(g) + e⁻
  3. Mg(g) → Mg²⁺(g) + 2e⁻
  4. Mg(g) + e⁻ → Mg⁻(g)

IE₁ is for gaseous atoms losing one electron to form 1+ ions. Option C is the sum of IE₁ and IE₂; option D is an electron affinity.

Electron affinity (EA)

DefinitionThe first electron affinity is the energy change when one mole of electrons is added to one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1− ions: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g).
  • First EAs are usually negative (exothermic), because the incoming electron is attracted to the nucleus. Second EAs are always positive: an electron is being forced onto an ion that is already negative (e.g. O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g) is endothermic).
  • Across a period, EA generally becomes more exothermic (greater nuclear charge, smaller atom). Halogens have the most exothermic values.
  • Down a group, EA generally becomes less exothermic (electron added further from the nucleus).
  • Anomaly: chlorine has a more exothermic EA than fluorine. Fluorine is so small that the added electron is repelled strongly by the electrons already in the crowded 2p sublevel.
  • Group 2 and group 18 elements have EAs that are close to zero or positive, because the electron must go into a new, higher-energy sublevel.
Common mistakeElectron affinity is not just "the energy to add an electron to an atom". It is an energy change (usually released, so negative), per mole, for gaseous atoms forming 1− ions.

Electronegativity

DefinitionElectronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract a shared pair of electrons in a covalent bond. It is measured on the Pauling scale (no units); fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0).
  • Increases across a period and decreases down a group (same reasons as IE).
  • Noble gases are usually not given values because they rarely form bonds.
  • The difference in electronegativity between two elements predicts the bond type (see Structure 2: bonding triangle).

One useful summary of the trend in electronegativity across period 3: Na 0.9 → Mg 1.3 → Al 1.6 → Si 1.9 → P 2.2 → S 2.6 → Cl 3.2.

Exam question: (a) define electronegativity [1]; (b) explain why atomic radius decreases across period 3 [2]

(a) The ability of an atom (nucleus) to attract a bonding/shared pair of electrons ✓. Do not write "element" instead of atom, or just "electrons".

(b) Increasing nuclear charge/number of protons, so increased attraction of the nucleus for the outer electrons ✓; the electrons are added to the same outer energy level, so shielding stays about the same ✓. Examiners noted that many students wrongly said the attraction increases because there are more electrons.

Summary of trends

PropertyAcross a period (left → right)Down a group
Atomic radiusDecreasesIncreases
Ionic radiusDecreases for cations, jumps up at the anions, then decreases againIncreases
First ionization energyGenerally increasesDecreases
Electron affinityGenerally more exothermicGenerally less exothermic
ElectronegativityIncreasesDecreases
Metallic characterDecreasesIncreases
Exam tip"Explain" questions on trends need all three ideas: what happens to nuclear charge, what happens to shielding/number of shells, and the effect on the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electrons. Writing only "the atom gets smaller" scores little. Never say electrons are "added to a new shell" across a period.

Fill the gap: going down a group, a new shell is added, so the outer electrons are further from the nucleus.

title: Period 3: melting points, metallic character and oxides
html:
Melting points across period 3

Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar: explain the trend in melting and boiling points. Hint: think about the type of bonding between atoms of the same element.

ElementsStructure and bondingMelting point trend
Na, Mg, AlMetallic lattice of cations in a sea of delocalized electronsIncreases Na < Mg < Al: higher ion charge (1+, 2+, 3+), smaller ion and more delocalized electrons → stronger metallic bonding
SiGiant covalent networkHighest: many strong covalent bonds must break
P₄, S₈, Cl₂Simple molecules held by London (dispersion) forcesLow; S₈ > P₄ > Cl₂ because bigger molecules have more electrons and stronger London forces
ArSingle atomsLowest: very weak London forces

Why does sulfur have a higher melting point than phosphorus?

  1. Sulfur has stronger covalent bonds within its molecules
  2. S₈ molecules have more electrons than P₄ molecules, so the London forces between them are stronger
  3. Sulfur is a giant covalent structure
  4. Sulfur has hydrogen bonding

Both are simple molecular. Melting overcomes only intermolecular forces; the larger S₈ molecule (128 electrons vs 60 in P₄) has stronger London forces. Covalent bonds inside the molecules are not broken.

Exam question: (a) state the structure of silicon and explain its very high melting point [3]; (b) explain why sulfur melts at a higher temperature than phosphorus [3]; (c) explain why aluminium is malleable, with a diagram of at least six particles [3]

(a) Giant covalent/macromolecular ✓; many strong covalent bonds ✓ must be broken, requiring a lot of energy ✓.

(b) Both are simple molecular ✓; the S₈ molecule is bigger/has more electrons than P₄ ✓, so the London (dispersion) forces are stronger and need more energy to overcome ✓. Do not say covalent bonds break.

(c) Diagram: a regular arrangement of 3+ ions (at least two rows) with delocalized electrons ✓; positive charge in each ion ✓; layers/rows of ions can slide over one another without breaking the metallic bond ✓.

S3.1.5 Metallic and non-metallic character

Metallic character is the tendency of an element to lose electrons (low IE, low electronegativity). It decreases across a period and increases down a group, so Cs is the most metallic element in common use and F the most non-metallic. Group 14 shows this well: C (non-metal) → Si, Ge (metalloids) → Sn, Pb (metals). Non-metallic character is the tendency to gain electrons; it follows the opposite trend.

Oxides of period 3

Oxides show the change from metal to non-metal across a period:

  • Metal oxides are basic. They are ionic; the O²⁻ ion accepts protons. Soluble ones form alkaline solutions; all neutralize acids.
  • Non-metal oxides are acidic. They are covalent and form acidic solutions in water or react with bases.
  • Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases, e.g. Al₂O₃ (also ZnO).

Equations: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O; 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO; 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃; Si + O₂ → SiO₂; 4P + 5O₂ → P₄O₁₀; S + O₂ → SO₂.

Period 3 oxideBonding / structureNatureEquation with water (or acid/base)pH of solution
Na₂OIonic latticeBasicNa₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH≈ 14
MgOIonic latticeBasicMgO + H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ (slightly soluble)≈ 9–10
Al₂O₃Ionic with covalent characterAmphotericInsoluble. Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2NaAl(OH)₄7
SiO₂Giant covalentAcidicInsoluble. SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O7
P₄O₁₀Simple molecularAcidicP₄O₁₀ + 6H₂O → 4H₃PO₄≈ 1–2
SO₂ / SO₃Simple molecularAcidicSO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄≈ 1–2

Ionic equations show the acid–base behaviour clearly. Basic oxide with acid: O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O (e.g. MgO + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂O). Amphoteric Al₂O₃ with alkali: Al₂O₃ + 2OH⁻ + 3H₂O → 2[Al(OH)₄]⁻. Acidic oxide with alkali: SiO₂ + 2OH⁻ → SiO₃²⁻ + H₂O; SO₃ + OH⁻ → HSO₄⁻; SO₂ + OH⁻ → HSO₃⁻.

Other acidic oxides to know: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid; causes ocean acidification and the natural pH ≈ 5.6 of rain) and the nitrogen oxides, 2NO₂ + H₂O → HNO₃ + HNO₂. Sulfur and nitrogen oxides from burning fuels and from car engines cause acid deposition (acid rain). CO and NO are neutral oxides.

Which oxide is amphoteric?

  1. Na₂O
  2. SiO₂
  3. SO₃
  4. Al₂O₃

Al₂O₃ reacts with acids (forming Al³⁺) and with alkalis (forming [Al(OH)₄]⁻). SiO₂ reacts only with bases; Na₂O only with acids; SO₃ only with bases.

Exam tipWhen asked to show that an oxide is amphoteric you must give two equations: one with an acid and one with a base. Simply writing "it reacts with acids and bases" usually scores 1 mark at most.
Exam question: samples of sodium oxide and sulfur trioxide are added to separate beakers of water. Deduce the equation for each and classify each oxide as acidic, basic or neutral [3]

Na₂O(s) + H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq): basic.
SO₃(l) + H₂O(l) → H₂SO₄(aq): acidic.

Linked question: P₄O₁₀ + 6H₂O → 4H₃PO₄; the NaOH solution has pH > 7 and the H₃PO₄ solution pH < 7.

Explain why sodium oxide has a higher melting point than sulfur trioxide [3]

Na₂O is ionic: strong electrostatic attraction between Na⁺ and O²⁻ throughout a giant lattice ✓. SO₃ is molecular: only weak intermolecular forces (London/dipole–dipole) between molecules ✓. Intermolecular forces are much weaker and more easily overcome than ionic bonds ✓.

title: Groups 1 and 17
html:
S3.1.4 Trends down a group: group 1 and group 17

Do now: why are group 1 elements (like sodium) and group 17 elements (like chlorine) so dangerous, while their compound sodium chloride is table salt? (Hint: one atom badly wants to lose an electron and the other badly wants to gain one. Once they have done so, both ions have stable noble-gas configurations.)

Group 1, the alkali metals

Group 1, the alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs) are soft, low-density metals with low melting points. They are stored under oil because they react with air and water.

  • All have one valence electron (ns¹), which they lose to form M⁺ ions. That is why they react in the same way.
  • Reactivity increases down the group: the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily (lower IE).
  • Melting point decreases down the group: larger ions with the same 1+ charge → weaker metallic bonding.
2M(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2MOH(aq) + H₂(g)    e.g. 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂

Observations with water: Li fizzes steadily; Na melts into a ball and darts around; K melts and the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame; Rb and Cs react explosively. The solution turns universal indicator purple (an alkaline hydroxide forms).

Why does potassium react more vigorously with water than sodium?

  1. Potassium has more protons, so it attracts water more strongly
  2. Potassium has a higher melting point
  3. Potassium's outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily
  4. Potassium has two outer electrons

Both lose one ns¹ electron. In K the electron is in the 4th shell, further away and more shielded, so its ionization energy is lower and it is lost more readily.

Exam question: (a) state the equation for sodium and water [1]; (b) state and explain one difference between the reactions of sodium and potassium with water [2]

(a) 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g) (fractional coefficients accepted).

(b) K reacts more vigorously / the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame / more heat is produced ✓; K loses its outer electron more readily (K is more reactive) because the electron is further from the nucleus ✓.

Other acceptable observations for sodium: fizzing/bubbles, sodium floats, melts into a ball and disappears, the temperature rises. Rate order: K > Na > Li.

2M(s) + X₂ → 2MX(s)    e.g. 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s)

Alkali metals react with halogens to form white ionic halide salts. The most vigorous reactions are between the metals at the bottom of group 1 and the halogens at the top of group 17.

Group 17, the halogens

Group 17, the halogens exist as diatomic molecules (X₂).

HalogenState and colour at room temperatureColour in waterColour in cyclohexane
F₂Pale yellow gas(reacts with water)—
Cl₂Yellow-green gasVery pale green / colourlessVery pale green / colourless
Br₂Red-brown liquidYellow-orangeOrange
I₂Grey-black solid (purple vapour)Yellow-brownViolet / purple
  • Melting and boiling points increase down the group: larger molecules with more electrons have stronger London forces.
  • Halogens have seven valence electrons (ns² np⁵) and gain one electron to form X⁻ ions, so they act as oxidizing agents.
  • Reactivity decreases down the group: the incoming electron goes into a shell further from the nucleus and is more shielded, so it is attracted less strongly.

Practical: displacement reactions of the halogens

Displacement reactions (your class practical): a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from a solution of its halide ions.

Method: wearing eye protection, put 2 drops of chlorine water, bromine water and iodine solution into separate rows of a dimple tile. Add one drop of cyclohexane to each (highly flammable and harmful: no flames). Record the colours. Then add 2 drops of potassium chloride, potassium bromide and potassium iodide solution (0.1 mol dm⁻³) to the three columns, using a clean pipette each time, and record the colours again.

How do you know which reactions show displacement? How could you have predicted this?

A colour change shows that a new halogen has been formed (orange Br₂ or brown I₂). You could predict it from reactivity: a halogen displaces any halide below it in group 17, because the higher halogen is the stronger oxidizing agent (it attracts an extra electron more strongly).

ReactionIonic equationObservation
Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂Colourless → yellow-orange (orange in cyclohexane)
Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂Colourless → brown (violet in cyclohexane)
Br₂ + 2KI → 2KBr + I₂Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂Orange → brown (violet in cyclohexane)
Br₂ + KCl, I₂ + KCl, I₂ + KBrNo reactionNo change

These are redox reactions. In Cl₂ + 2Br⁻, chlorine is reduced (0 → −1) and is the oxidizing agent; bromide is oxidized (−1 → 0) and is the reducing agent. K⁺ is a spectator ion. Fluorine is not used in aqueous displacement because it reacts with water.

Common mistakeAdding cyclohexane is how you tell bromine and iodine apart: both look brownish in water, but iodine turns the organic layer violet, while bromine turns it orange.

Which statement about the elements in group 17 is correct?

  1. Br₂ will oxidize Cl⁻
  2. F₂ has the least tendency to be reduced
  3. Cl₂ will oxidize I⁻
  4. I₂ is a stronger oxidizing agent than F₂

Oxidizing strength decreases down the group, so Cl₂ (higher) oxidizes I⁻ (lower) to I₂. Br₂ cannot oxidize Cl⁻; F₂ is the most easily reduced; I₂ is the weakest oxidizing agent.

Will a reaction happen? Which pair reacts?

  1. Bromine + potassium fluoride
  2. Chlorine + sodium iodide
  3. Iodine + calcium bromide
  4. Bromine + potassium chloride

Only a halogen higher in the group displaces a lower halide. Cl₂ + 2NaI → 2NaCl + I₂. The other three would need a lower halogen to displace a higher one. (Fluorine + lithium chloride would react in principle, but F₂ reacts with water so it is not done in solution.)

Exam question: (i) describe the colour change when aqueous chlorine is added to aqueous sodium bromide [1]; (ii) explain, with an equation, why it occurs [2]; (iii) what is seen with excess chlorine and sodium iodide? [1]

(i) From (pale) green/colourless to yellow/orange/brown. The initial colour must be stated.

(ii) Chlorine is a more powerful oxidizing agent than bromine (or bromide is a stronger reducing agent than chloride) ✓; Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → Br₂(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq) ✓.

(iii) A (dark) solid forms in a colourless solution, or a dark brown solution.

Exam question: chlorine gas is bubbled separately through aqueous bromine, Br₂(aq), and potassium bromide, KBr(aq). Predict the observations

Br₂(aq): no change (there is no bromide to oxidize). KBr(aq): colour change from colourless to yellow/orange/brown as Br₂ forms.

title: Oxidation states
html:
S3.1.6 Oxidation states

Do now: produce a quick mind map of all the periodicity trends you have covered so far.

Oxidation and reduction used to mean the addition or removal of oxygen (rusting is oxidation of iron). Now we use them to describe the movement of electrons. If electrons move during a reaction, one species is oxidized while another is reduced: hence redox.

Instead of tracking where electrons have gone, we can see whether something has been oxidized or reduced by looking at its oxidation state. Every element in a compound has an oxidation state.

DefinitionThe oxidation state is the charge an atom would have if all its bonds were fully ionic (shared electrons given to the more electronegative atom). It is written with the sign first (+2, −1). An increase in oxidation state is oxidation; a decrease is reduction.

Rules (apply them in order):

  1. An uncombined element has oxidation state 0 (Na, O₂, Cl₂, S₈): the bonded atoms are identical, so no electrons are transferred between them.
  2. For a monatomic ion, the oxidation state equals the charge (Fe³⁺ = +3).
  3. The oxidation states in a neutral compound add up to 0; in a polyatomic ion they add up to the charge of the ion.
  4. Fluorine is always −1. Group 1 is always +1, group 2 always +2, aluminium +3.
  5. Hydrogen is +1, except in metal hydrides (NaH), where it is −1.
  6. Oxygen is −2, except in peroxides (H₂O₂, Na₂O₂: −1) and in OF₂ (+2).
  7. Chlorine is −1, except when bonded to O or F, when it is positive.

In a binary compound, the more electronegative element is given the (negative) oxidation state it would have as an ion.

Worked exampleFind the oxidation state of the underlined atom.
(a) CO₃²⁻: 3 × (−2) = −6; total −2 → C = +4.
(b) Cl₂O₃ (covalent, not ionic!): 3 × (−2) = −6; total 0 → 2Cl = +6 → Cl = +3.
(c) Cr₂O₇²⁻: 7 × (−2) = −14; total −2 → 2Cr = +12 → Cr = +6.
(d) SOCl₂: Cl = −1 each, O = −2 → S = +4.
(e) NH₄Cl: NH₄⁺ has charge +1; 4 × (+1) = +4 → N = −3.
(f) PbCl₄: 4 × (−1) = −4; total 0 → Pb = +4.

What is the oxidation state of P in H₃PO₄? (Type the number; +5 is entered as 5.)

H = +1 (×3 = +3), O = −2 (×4 = −8). Sum must be 0: P + 3 − 8 = 0, so P = +5.

What is the oxidation state of Mn in MnO₄⁻?

4 × (−2) = −8. The ion has charge −1, so Mn − 8 = −1 → Mn = +7.
Work out the oxidation states in: CH₄, PCl₃, NCl₃, CS₂, ICl₅, BrF₃, PCl₄⁺, H₃PO₄, NH₄Cl, H₂SO₄, MgCO₃, SOCl₂

CH₄: C −4, H +1 · PCl₃: P +3, Cl −1 · NCl₃: N +3, Cl −1 (Cl, 3.2, is more electronegative than N, 3.0) · CS₂: C +4, S −2 · ICl₅: I +5, Cl −1 · BrF₃: Br +3, F −1 · PCl₄⁺: P +5, Cl −1 · H₃PO₄: H +1, P +5, O −2 · NH₄Cl: N −3, H +1, Cl −1 · H₂SO₄: H +1, S +6, O −2 · MgCO₃: Mg +2, C +4, O −2 · SOCl₂: S +4, O −2, Cl −1

Give the oxidation state of: (a) S in SO, SO₂, SO₃, SO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻; (b) Cl in ClO₂, ClO⁻, ClO₂⁻, ClO₃⁻, ClO₄⁻; (c) N in N₂O, NO, NO₂, N₂O₄, N₂O₅, NO₂⁻, NO₃⁻

(a) +2, +4, +6, +4, +6
(b) +4, +1, +3, +5, +7
(c) +1, +2, +4, +4, +5, +3, +5

Give the oxidation state of: (a) S in H₂S, S, H₂SO₄, S²⁻, HS⁻, SO₂, SO₃; (b) P in HPO₃, H₃PO₂, H₃PO₃, H₃PO₄, H₄P₂O₇, H₅P₃O₁₀

(a) −2, 0, +6, −2, −2, +4, +6
(b) +5, +1, +3, +5, +5, +5

Underlined atoms: Cs₂O, PtCl₆²⁻, CaI₂, SnF₂, Al₂O₃, ClF₃, H₃AsO₃, SbF₆⁻, TiO₂, P₄, MoO₄²⁻, MnO₄⁻, PtCl₄²⁻, O₂, O₃ (the first element in each)

Cs +1 · Pt +4 · Ca +2 · Sn +2 · Al +3 · Cl +3 · As +3 · Sb +5 · Ti +4 · P 0 · Mo +6 · Mn +7 · Pt +2 · O 0 · O 0

Naming with Roman numerals

Naming with Roman numerals: the Roman numeral in a name is the oxidation state of the element: iron(III) chloride is FeCl₃; manganese(IV) oxide is MnO₂; PbO₂ is lead(IV) oxide; SnCl₂ is tin(II) chloride; TiCl₄ is titanium(IV) chloride; Cr₂O₇²⁻ is dichromate(VI). Copper forms copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O, and copper(II) oxide, CuO. IUPAC calls the Roman numeral the oxidation number, so the two terms are often used interchangeably. More examples: SO₃ is sulfur(VI) oxide; PCl₅ is phosphorus(V) chloride and PCl₃ phosphorus(III) chloride; SbCl₃ is antimony(III) chloride; BrF₅ is bromine(V) fluoride.

What is the name of Cr₂O₃?

  1. Chromium(III) oxide
  2. Chromium(II) oxide
  3. Chromium(VI) oxide
  4. Dichromium trioxide(II)

3 × (−2) = −6 shared between two Cr atoms, so each Cr is +3: chromium(III) oxide.

Redox reactions and oxidation states

In any reaction where one species is oxidized (loses electrons), another must be reduced (gains electrons). The oxidizing agent removes electrons from another species and is itself reduced; the reducing agent gives electrons to another species and is itself oxidized. Only redox reactions involve a change in oxidation state.

Which reaction is not a redox reaction?

  1. CO₂ + H₂ → CO + H₂O
  2. Pb(NO₃)₂ + Na₂SO₄ → 2NaNO₃ + PbSO₄
  3. 2Al + 3Ni(NO₃)₂ → 2Al(NO₃)₃ + 3Ni
  4. 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO

In the precipitation reaction every element keeps its oxidation state (Pb +2, N +5, O −2, Na +1, S +6). In A, C goes +4 → +2 and H 0 → +1; in C, Al 0 → +3 and Ni +2 → 0.

Disproportionation is when the same element is both oxidized and reduced in one reaction, e.g. Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl (Cl: 0 → −1 and 0 → +1); 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ (O: −1 → −2 and −1 → 0); Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O (Cl: 0 → −1 and 0 → +1).

Classify each reaction (redox? disproportionation? oxidizing and reducing agents): (1) Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH; (2) 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃; (3) 2NaBr + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2HBr; (4) 2KBr + F₂ → Br₂ + 2KF; (5) 2Cl₂ + 2H₂O → 4HCl + O₂; (6) 3MnO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ → 2MnO₄⁻ + MnO₂ + 2H₂O
  1. Not redox (no changes).
  2. Redox: S +4 → +6 (SO₂ oxidized, reducing agent); O 0 → −2 (O₂ oxidizing agent).
  3. Not redox: an acid–base reaction.
  4. Redox: Br −1 → 0 (Br⁻ is the reducing agent); F 0 → −1 (F₂ is the oxidizing agent).
  5. Redox, not disproportionation: Cl 0 → −1 (Cl₂ is the oxidizing agent); O −2 → 0 (H₂O is the reducing agent).
  6. Disproportionation: Mn +6 → +7 and +6 → +4; MnO₄²⁻ is both oxidizing and reducing agent.
Common mistakeOxidation states are per atom. In Cr₂O₇²⁻ the oxidation state of Cr is +6, not +12. And a charge is written 2+, while an oxidation state is written +2.

title: Discontinuities in first ionization energy (AHL)
html:
S3.1.7 Discontinuities in the trend of first ionization energy AHL

Do now: why do elements react? What types of substances do they form once they have reacted? Evidence for how electrons are arranged in atoms comes from ionization energies.

Reminder from S1.3: IE₁ is the energy to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms (Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻). The 2nd IE removes the second electron from the 1+ ion (Na⁺(g) → Na²⁺(g) + e⁻), not both electrons. IE depends on atomic radius, nuclear charge and shielding.

Common mistakeKeep shell, sublevel and orbital separate: a shell (n = 3) contains sublevels (3s, 3p, 3d) and a sublevel contains orbitals (3p has three). Also remember that 4s fills before 3d in atoms, but 4s empties before 3d when ions form.
Task: match each first IE (kJ mol⁻¹) to its period 3 group: 786, 738, 1012, 496, 1521, 578, 1000, 1251. Then reveal
IE₁ / kJ mol⁻¹Element (group)
496Na (1)
738Mg (2)
578Al (13)
786Si (14)
1012P (15)
1000S (16)
1251Cl (17)
1521Ar (18)

The lowest value is the group 1 metal and the highest the noble gas. The tricky ones are Al (lower than Mg) and S (lower than P).

First IEs across period 3 (kJ mol⁻¹): Na 496, Mg 738, Al 578, Si 786, P 1012, S 1000, Cl 1251, Ar 1521. The general increase has two dips, at Al and S. The same pattern appears in period 2 at B and O.

  • Mg → Al (and Be → B): the electron removed from Al is in the 3p sublevel ([Ne] 3s² 3p¹), which is higher in energy than 3s and is partly shielded by the 3s electrons. So it is easier to remove than an electron from Mg's 3s sublevel.
  • P → S (and N → O): phosphorus has three unpaired 3p electrons (↿ ↿ ↿). In sulfur (↿⇂ ↿ ↿) the fourth 3p electron must pair up in an orbital that is already occupied. The extra repulsion between the paired electrons makes one of them easier to remove.

Why is the first ionization energy of aluminium lower than that of magnesium?

  1. Al has fewer protons than Mg
  2. Al has a paired electron in a 3p orbital
  3. Al's outer electron is in a new shell
  4. Al's outer electron is in the 3p sublevel, which is higher in energy than 3s

Al has more protons, and its outer electron is still in shell 3. But it is in 3p, a higher-energy sublevel, partly shielded by the 3s² pair, so less energy is needed. Spin-pair repulsion explains the S dip, not Al.

Which pair shows a decrease in IE₁ caused by spin-pair repulsion?

  1. N → O
  2. Be → B
  3. Ne → Na
  4. C → N

O (2p⁴) has the first paired 2p electron, which is repelled by its partner and is easier to remove. Be → B is the s → p effect; Ne → Na is a new shell; C → N is a normal increase.

Exam tipThese dips are evidence for sublevels. In an explanation, name the sublevels (3s vs 3p) and say "spin-pair repulsion" or "electron pairing in a 3p orbital". The reverse question (why Al's IE is lower than Mg's even though Al has more protons) needs the same argument.
Exam question: (a) define first ionization energy [2]; (b) explain why the first IE of magnesium is higher than that of sodium [2]

(a) The (minimum) energy required to remove one (mole of) electron(s) ✓ from (one mole of) atoms in the gaseous state ✓.

(b) Mg has a greater nuclear charge/more protons ✓, so there is greater attraction for electrons in the same shell / Mg has a smaller atomic radius ✓.

Related: calcium has a higher melting point than potassium because Ca²⁺ has twice the charge of K⁺ and Ca gives more delocalized electrons, so the attraction between the cations and the delocalized electrons is greater.

Successive IEs and their link to group number are covered in Structure 1.3 (AHL): a big jump appears when an electron is removed from a new, inner shell.

By how much does IE₁ drop from P (1012 kJ mol⁻¹) to S (1000 kJ mol⁻¹)?

1012 − 1000 = 12 kJ mol⁻¹. Compare the Mg → Al drop: 738 − 578 = 160 kJ mol⁻¹. The pairing effect is small; the s → p effect is much larger.

title: Transition elements and variable oxidation states (AHL)
html:
S3.1.8 Transition elements and their properties AHL

What is different about the transition elements compared with other elements? Look at some examples (copper, iron, titanium, silver, gold, platinum) and try to list properties that fit them all.

DefinitionA transition element is an element that has an incomplete d sublevel in the atom or in one or more of its common ions.
  • All transition elements are in the d-block, but not all d-block elements are transition elements. Scandium forms only Sc³⁺ ([Ar], no d electrons) and zinc forms only Zn²⁺ ([Ar] 3d¹⁰, a full d sublevel), so neither is a transition element. In the first row, the transition elements run from Ti to Cu.
  • When transition metals form ions, the 4s electrons are lost before the 3d electrons: Fe [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² → Fe²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁶ → Fe³⁺ [Ar] 3d⁵.

Characteristic properties (all linked to the partly filled d sublevel):

  1. Variable oxidation states, e.g. Fe +2/+3, Cu +1/+2, Mn from +2 to +7.
  2. Formation of complex ions with ligands, e.g. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺.
  3. Coloured compounds and solutions, e.g. Cu²⁺(aq) blue, Fe²⁺(aq) pale green, Fe³⁺(aq) yellow-orange, Ni²⁺ green, Cr³⁺ green, MnO₄⁻ purple. Compounds of Sc³⁺ and Zn²⁺ are white/colourless.
  4. Catalytic activity, e.g. Fe in the Haber process, V₂O₅ in the Contact process, Ni in the hydrogenation of alkenes, MnO₂ in the decomposition of H₂O₂, Pt/Pd/Rh in catalytic converters.
  5. Magnetic properties due to unpaired d electrons.
  6. Typical metal properties, but more strongly than group 1: high melting points and densities, hard and strong, good conductors (both the 4s and 3d electrons are delocalized). Mercury is the exception (liquid at room temperature).

Transition metals are much less reactive than group 1: copper has to be heated strongly to react with oxygen, and iron rusts only slowly compared with how fast sodium reacts with water. That slowness makes them useful for building materials and jewellery, although rusting of iron can weaken structures. Further coloured compounds: copper(II) sulfate is blue (Cu²⁺), nickel(II) carbonate pale green (Ni²⁺), chromium(III) oxide dark green (Cr³⁺) and manganese(II) chloride pale pink (Mn²⁺). Vanadium shows four colours in solution as its oxidation state changes: +5 yellow (VO₂⁺), +4 blue (VO²⁺), +3 green (V³⁺) and +2 violet (V²⁺).

Catalysis: transition metals can act as heterogeneous catalysts (in a different phase, usually a solid surface that adsorbs the gas or liquid reactants, weakens their bonds and holds them in a good position to react) or homogeneous catalysts (in the same phase, usually ions in solution that change oxidation state and back again, e.g. Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺). Both provide an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.

Magnetism:

  • Diamagnetic substances have only paired electrons and are weakly repelled by a magnetic field (e.g. Zn²⁺, Sc³⁺, Cu⁺).
  • Paramagnetic substances have unpaired electrons and are attracted into a magnetic field; more unpaired electrons give a stronger effect (Fe³⁺, 3d⁵, with five unpaired electrons, is strongly paramagnetic).
  • Ferromagnetism (Fe, Co, Ni) is the strongest effect: unpaired electrons in neighbouring atoms line up in domains and stay aligned when the field is removed, giving permanent magnets.

Which ion is paramagnetic?

  1. Zn²⁺
  2. Sc³⁺
  3. Fe²⁺
  4. Cu⁺

Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶ with four unpaired electrons. Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰), Sc³⁺ (3d⁰) and Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) have all electrons paired, so they are diamagnetic.

Exam questions: (1) state how mercury is unlike a typical transition metal; (2) name FeCl₂, Cr₂O₃, MnBr₂, NiCO₃; (3) give the names and formulas of the two oxides of copper

(1) Mercury is a liquid at room temperature (very low melting point).

(2) Iron(II) chloride; chromium(III) oxide; manganese(II) bromide; nickel(II) carbonate.

(3) Copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O, and copper(II) oxide, CuO.

S3.1.9 Variable oxidation states AHL

The 4s and 3d sublevels are very close in energy, so the successive ionization energies of transition elements increase gradually with no large jump until all the 4s and 3d electrons have gone. Losing different numbers of electrons therefore needs similar amounts of energy, and the energy can be recovered from lattice or hydration enthalpy or covalent bond formation. In contrast, for Mg there is a huge jump after the second IE, so Mg only forms Mg²⁺.

  • Almost all first-row transition metals form a +2 state (loss of both 4s electrons).
  • The maximum oxidation state rises to manganese (+7 = all 4s and 3d electrons) and then falls.
  • Higher oxidation states usually occur in oxyanions or compounds with very electronegative O or F: MnO₄⁻ (+7), Cr₂O₇²⁻ and CrO₄²⁻ (+6), VO₂⁺ (+5).

What is the oxidation state of Mn in MnO₄²⁻?

4 × (−2) = −8; overall charge −2, so Mn = −2 + 8 = +6. In MnO₄⁻ it is +7.
Worked exampleGive the full electron configurations of Cr³⁺ and Cu⁺.
Cr: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹. Remove the 4s electron first, then two 3d: Cr³⁺ = [Ar] 3d³ (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d³).
Cu: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Remove 4s¹: Cu⁺ = [Ar] 3d¹⁰. Because its d sublevel is full, Cu⁺ compounds are colourless and diamagnetic.
Check your understanding: (1) which first-row element shows the most oxidation states? (2) which two first-row d-block elements are not transition elements? (3) why does the number of oxidation states rise towards the middle of the row?

(1) Manganese (+2 to +7).

(2) Scandium and zinc.

(3) Up to Mn, each element has more 4s + 3d electrons that are close in energy and can be lost or used in bonding; after Mn the increasing nuclear charge holds the 3d electrons more tightly, so the highest states become less accessible.

title: Complex ions, d-orbital splitting and colour (AHL)
html:
S3.1.10–S3.1.11 Complex ions, d-orbital splitting and colour AHL

Starter: write down the properties of transition metals (high melting point; conduct heat and electricity, so they are used for furnaces and jet engines; strong, so they are used in construction).

Complex ions: transition metal ions are small and highly charged, so they act as Lewis acids: they accept electron pairs from ligands (Lewis bases) to form coordination (dative) bonds. A complex has the metal ion in the centre, surrounded by ligands.

DefinitionA ligand is a molecule or ion with a lone pair that it donates to a central metal ion to form a coordination bond. The coordination number is the number of coordination bonds to the central ion.
  • Monodentate ligands form one bond: H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, OH⁻, CN⁻. Bidentate ligands form two: ethane-1,2-diamine (en), H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂; ethanedioate C₂O₄²⁻. Polydentate ligands form several: EDTA⁴⁻ forms six (it is used to treat lead poisoning); haem holds Fe²⁺ in haemoglobin. Multidentate ligands are also called chelating ligands (from the Greek for "claw").
  • Shapes: coordination number 6 → octahedral ([Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺); 4 → tetrahedral (with large ligands, e.g. [CuCl₄]²⁻) or square planar (cisplatin, [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]); 2 → linear ([Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, Tollens' reagent).

Small ligands such as H₂O and NH₃ fit six around the metal; larger ones such as Cl⁻ usually fit only four. An octahedral complex can also hold three bidentate ligands, as in [Ni(en)₃]²⁺. The chelate effect: a bidentate or polydentate ligand readily replaces monodentate ligands, because one ligand replaces several and the number of free particles increases.

In haemoglobin, the Fe²⁺ in each haem group binds O₂ and carries it around the body. Carbon monoxide is toxic because it binds to this Fe²⁺ much more strongly than O₂ does. (Cyanide is toxic mainly because it binds to the iron in an enzyme of respiration, cytochrome c oxidase.)

What is the coordination number of the metal in [Cu(en)₂(H₂O)₂]²⁺? (en = ethane-1,2-diamine, a bidentate ligand)

  1. 2
  2. 4
  3. 5
  4. 6

Each en forms two coordination bonds (2 × 2 = 4) and each water one (2 × 1 = 2): 6 in total, so the complex is octahedral.

Worked exampleDeduce the oxidation state of the metal in (a) [CuCl₄]²⁻ and (b) [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺.
(a) 4 × Cl⁻ = −4; overall −2 → Cu = +2.
(b) NH₃ is neutral; 2 × Cl⁻ = −2; overall +1 → Co = +3. The coordination number is 6 (octahedral).

Charges of complexes: if the ligands are neutral (H₂O), the complex has the charge of the metal ion: Cu²⁺ + 6H₂O → [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺. If two of the ligands are OH⁻, the charges cancel: [Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄] is neutral.

Cisplatin is [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], a neutral square planar complex. What is the oxidation state of Pt?

NH₃ is neutral; 2 × Cl⁻ = −2; overall 0, so Pt = +2.

Why complexes are coloured: d-orbital splitting

Transition metal ions are coloured, in solution or in complexes, whereas most other metal ions (Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺) are colourless.

  1. In a free ion, the five 3d orbitals are degenerate (equal energy).
  2. When ligands approach, their lone pairs repel the d electrons. The d orbitals pointing towards the ligands are repelled more than the others, so the d sublevel splits into two sets with an energy gap ΔE (in an octahedral complex: two higher, three lower).
  3. An electron in the lower set absorbs a photon of visible light with exactly the energy ΔE (ΔE = hf = hc/λ) and is promoted to the upper set.
  4. The remaining wavelengths are transmitted or reflected; we see the complementary colour of the light absorbed (use the colour wheel in the data booklet).

Why the complementary colour? The eye sees a mixture of all colours in the proportions in sunlight as white. Two complementary colours together also look white, so when one colour is removed from white light, the eye sees its complement. If red is absorbed we see green; if violet is absorbed we see yellow.

Example: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ absorbs orange-red light (around 600–700 nm), so it appears blue. Blue light is not emitted; it is what is left over.

Key pointA complex is only coloured if the d sublevel is partly filled. With d⁰ (Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺) there is no electron to promote; with d¹⁰ (Zn²⁺, Cu⁺) there is no empty space in the upper set. So these ions are colourless.

A solution absorbs mainly yellow light. Which colour does it appear?

  1. Yellow
  2. Violet
  3. Green
  4. Orange

We see the complementary colour of the light absorbed. On the colour wheel, yellow is opposite violet.

Factors that change ΔE, and therefore the colour:

  • Identity of the metal (nuclear charge): different metals with the same charge and ligands, e.g. Mn²⁺ and Fe³⁺ (both d⁵), give different splitting.
  • Oxidation state of the metal: a higher charge pulls the ligands closer, so ΔE increases, e.g. [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ has a bigger splitting than [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺.
  • Identity of the ligand (spectrochemical series in the data booklet): ligands with a higher charge density on the donor atom split the d orbitals more.
    I⁻ < Br⁻ < S²⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < H₂O < SCN⁻ < NH₃ < CN⁻ < CO
    "Weak-field" ligands on the left give a small ΔE; "strong-field" ligands on the right give a large ΔE.
  • Geometry (coordination number): a tetrahedral complex has a smaller splitting than an octahedral one with the same ligands.
Worked exampleAdding excess ammonia to pale blue [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ gives deep blue-violet [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺. Explain the change.
1. NH₃ is above H₂O in the spectrochemical series, so it is a stronger-field ligand.
2. The splitting ΔE increases, so the complex absorbs light of higher energy (shorter wavelength): the absorption maximum moves from the red end of the spectrum towards orange-yellow.
3. The complementary colour observed therefore shifts from pale blue to a deeper blue-violet.
Exam tipBigger ΔE → absorbs higher energy, shorter wavelength light. You do not need to remember specific colours of complexes; you do need to use the colour wheel and explain direction of change.

Which change increases ΔE for an iron complex?

  1. Replacing H₂O ligands with CN⁻ ligands
  2. Replacing H₂O ligands with Cl⁻ ligands
  3. Reducing Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺
  4. Changing from octahedral to tetrahedral geometry

CN⁻ is a much stronger-field ligand than H₂O. Cl⁻ is weaker; a lower oxidation state and a tetrahedral geometry both give smaller splitting.

Colorimetry (useful for IAs): a colorimeter shines light of the colour the solution absorbs (complementary to the colour seen) through the sample and measures absorbance. A calibration curve of absorbance against known concentrations lets you find the concentration of an unknown solution. The reference (blank) is the pure solvent. A spectrophotometer scans many wavelengths and records which are absorbed or transmitted; for most IA work a colorimeter is enough.

You want to measure the concentration of Cu²⁺(aq) by colorimetry. Which filter colour should you choose, and how do you use a calibration curve?

Cu²⁺(aq) looks blue because it absorbs orange-red light, so choose an orange/red filter (the complementary colour). Measure the absorbance of several solutions of known concentration at regular intervals, plot absorbance against concentration, then read the unknown's concentration from its absorbance.
